original_question: Let n >= 3 and let Omega be an open subset of R^n. If f: Omega -> R^n is a homeomorphism that belongs to the Sobolev space W^{1,p}(Omega, R^n), is it true that f can be approximated in the W^{1,p} Sobolev norm by a sequence of diffeomorphisms, or by a sequence of piecewise affine homeomorphisms? Determine whether the answer depends on the exponent p, including whether positive results hold for all p or only in ranges such as p > n - 1, and whether counterexamples exist for smaller p.
target_in_paper: Section 2, Open problem 1 ("Ball-Evans problem in dimension n"), read with the immediately surrounding context from Theorem 2.1, Open problem 2, Theorem 2.2, and Open problem 3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s main higher-dimensional Ball-Evans approximation question: the setting n≥3, an open set Ω⊂R^n, a Sobolev homeomorphism in W^{1,p}, approximation in the W^{1,p} norm, and the two natural approximation classes of diffeomorphisms and piecewise affine homeomorphisms. It also correctly senses that the exponent p matters through known planar positive results, the special heuristic role of p>n−1, and known small-p obstructions.
missing_details: The nearest official formulation in the paper is a prove-or-disprove question in higher dimensions, stated as Open problem 1 in Section 2; it is not phrased as a complete classification over all exponents p.
The map should be described as a homeomorphism f:Ω→f(Ω)⊂R^n, not necessarily onto all of R^n.
The paper emphasizes that the problem is especially important in the physically relevant dimension n=3.
The approximation is asked in the W^{1,p}(Ω,R^n) Sobolev norm, not merely locally.
In higher dimensions the diffeomorphic-approximation question and the piecewise-affine-approximation question are distinct; the paper does not treat them as equivalent there.
The only equivalence discussion nearby is partial: diffeomorphic approximation implies piecewise affine approximation in any dimension, while the converse is proved only in the planar case.
The remark about p>n−1 (and possibly p=n−1) is only a heuristic about where a proof might be easier, not an established positive theorem.
The exact known counterexample range from Theorem 2.2 is n≥4 and 1≤p<⌊n/2⌋, via homeomorphisms whose Jacobian changes sign on sets of positive measure.
The paper separately isolates as Open problem 3 whether any further counterexample exists for some p in the remaining higher-dimensional range outside the known small-p regime.
The surrounding discussion records that the planar case is already settled positively, combining the previously known p>1 case with the later p=1 result.
refined_question: Fix n≥3, p∈[1,∞), an open set Ω⊂R^n, and a homeomorphism f:Ω→f(Ω)⊂R^n with f∈W^{1,p}(Ω,R^n). Prove or disprove that f can be approximated in the W^{1,p}(Ω,R^n)-norm by a sequence of smooth diffeomorphisms f_j:Ω→f_j(Ω)⊂R^n. Separately, ask the analogous question with smooth diffeomorphisms replaced by piecewise affine homeomorphisms. In particular, is this true in the physically relevant case n=3?
justification: Section 1 defines the Ball-Evans approximation problem as approximation of a Sobolev homeomorphism by diffeomorphisms or piecewise affine homeomorphisms in the Sobolev norm. Section 2 then gives the exact higher-dimensional formulation your draft is aiming at as Open problem 1, immediately after recalling the planar positive theorem. The nearby context matters: Open problem 2 explains that the diffeomorphic and piecewise-affine versions are not known equivalent in higher dimensions; Theorem 2.2 records the exact known small-p obstruction; and Open problem 3 isolates the remaining question of further counterexamples. The paper does not contain a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3 matching your draft, so Section 2 is the correct official target.
